speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understand that with the consent of the House no motion is necessary. If the House does not consent, the motion will have to be made.

We are for the first time applying the rule which was adopted last session in regard to going into Committee of Supply, and which is a departure from the rule formerly in existence. Before we proceed, I would like to ask my right hon. friend the Prime Minister for his understanding of the rule, so that we may know in the future exactly the position we are in. The rule reads as follows:
On Thursdays and Fridays when the Order of the Day is called for the House to go into Committee of Supply, or of Ways and Means, Mr. Speaker will leave the Chair without putting any question, provided that . . . the Estimates of each department shall be first taken up on a day other than Thursday or Friday.
My understanding of the rule is that if the House is moved into Committee of Supply on a day other than Thursday or Friday, and if at the conclusion of the day the subject matter of the department under consideration has not been exhausted, then when the House goes into Committee of Supply on Thursday or Friday, Mr. Speaker leaves the Chair without any motion. My understanding is that when you commence the consideration of the Estimates of a department, it must be done by the making of a motion. To-day we have no department whose estimates we have commenced, and therefore my right hon. friend the Prime Minister has moved the House into Committee of Supply. If we had commenced on a department on a day previous to to-day, Mr. Speaker would have left the Chair without any motion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: For the purpose of the estimates of that department.

For the purpose of the department. In other words, I take this to mean that the consideration of the Estimates of any department must be first commenced by a motion, and, if not finished within the day, it goes on automatically, Mr. Speaker leaves the Chair, and it is taken up again on Thursday or Friday.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That seems to be the understanding.

Then, as that seems to be the understanding, what are we to understand by the word 'department' which is used in this rule:
On Thursdays and Fridays, when the Order of the Day is called for the House to go into Committee of Supply, or of Ways and Means, Mr. Sneaker will leave the Chair without put-20i
ting any question, provided that, except by the consent of the House, the Estimates of each department shall be first taken up on a day other than Thursday or Friday.
To-day I understand we are taking up Civil Government, and taking it up as one department. On page 8 of the Estimates we have these words, 'Civil Government, amount to be voted, $6,413,378.75.' That is what is required for Civil Government. In this amount is included the expenditures of the various departments for the Civil Service at Ottawa; for instance, there is for the Customs Department $615,987, and again on page 96 we have another vote, item 342, amounting to $4,210,000, for the Customs Department. If we take up to-day all the departments and exhaust them, I suppose this will not be considered as having gone into the Interior or Customs or Excise or any other department, but that when the time comes for us to consider these appropriations, the House will have to be moved again into Committee of Supply?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I understand it very
much in the way that my right hon. friend understands it, except that I think he has perhaps construed the rule a little too favourably to the Government, if I apprehend him correctly.
I am too generous to the Government; it is a fault of mine.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Only unintentionally. I would think that every one of the departments which are enumerated, commencing at page 8, would be regarded as a separate department, and not as one department, as the light hon. gentleman suggests. In so far as I understand the construction of the rule, I think there is no difference of opinion between himself and myself. I would further say that we are taking this up practically by consent to-day, as the Government could not reasonably ask hon gentlemen to go on except by consent, and I would not regard any commencement that we may make to-day as bringing the case within the operation of the rule. We must bring each one of these departments before the House on some other day before we can make use of the rule in regard to Thursday and Friday.
Other than Thursday or Friday?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Other than Thursday or Friday. I think that is quite fair and reasonable, and I assent to it at once.

The Government revenue steam tug Alert, which is owned by a Sydney real estate broker and incidentally' receives the princely sum of $18,000 per y'ear of the people's money, was pressed into service yesterday to convey Tory organizer Hayes and Tory candidate Philip McLeod from North Sydney to the northern parts of Victoria county. The primary object of establishing this branch of the preventive service was to put a stop to the traffic of contraband liquor into Cape Breton seaports. Notwithstanding all this some of the barrels placed on board of the Government boat on its northward journey looked uncommonly like vessels containing ordinary booze. But although taken from a bonded warehouse and conveyed on board the ship by a teamster employed by a wholesale liquor dealer, they might have contained nothing more harmful than tomatoes of the Colchester county brand. In any event it is safe to say that the Government never intended to furnish Mr. Philip McLeod with a private yacht for electioneering purposes, even if he is the Tory candidate for Victoria county.
For the information of the House I may say than an election for a member for the local legislature of the piovince of Nova Scotia is taking place in that county and the election will be held on the i2th day of February. My only intention in reading this article is to bring it to the attention of the Government, or I suppose, more particularly of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fish-eiies (Mr. Hazen). He is not in his place at the present time, but I would be glad if he would tell this House whether or not the tug Alert, which is in the Government service, has gone to either one of the ports of Victoria county on an electioneering service and whether or not she has been ordered there by the department. If the hon. gentleman does not know these facts, I would ask him to have an investigation made and to give an answer to the House later.

I am addressing my re-ma ks to the Minister of Railways. I h ve letter^ irom the most reputable and largest business men in the province asking me to bring this nia.ter to the a.tention of the Government. Carvell Brothers, the largest wholesale business men in Charlottetown, and who I th.nk are supp rters of tie present Administration communicated with me on this matter, as have also M ssrs. Poole and Thomp on of Montague who do a large produce business. I quote a paragraph from a letter rec.ived f.om this firm:
In addition to the above we are informed that all freight rates on the Prince Edward Island railway have been advanced, except on Mussle mud, and the rates on cordwood, lumber, coal, hay and straw, lime, limestone, cement, brick, sand, gravel, stone, live stock, fertilizer, &c., are practically prohibitive, and will certainly result in loss of business for the railway as well as tying up the commerce of the country.
That is a condition of affairs that ought to be looked into. I am surprised that the Government did not take more heed of the representations made by their supporters in this House and by the delegations that have come from Prince Edward Island to interview them on this subject. The Prime Minister will remember that he visited Prince Edward Island shortly before the last Dominion election, and he held meetings there which were largely attended. There was a meeting held at Souris, the town in which I live, and the day being fine the meeting was held in a field, and it was largely attended by farmers and others. The Prime Minister referred to the grievances under which the people of the province were labouring in the matter of transporting their products. The right hon. gentleman stated that if he should come into power, one of the first things to which his Government would address its attention would be to redress these grievances. Well, there has been no redress in the line of reduction of rates, but on the contrary the rates have been increased. That is why I make a special appeal to the Prime Minister. I am quite sure he made that statement and that promise in good faith, and I am also sure the people who listened to him thought
it was in good faith. And yet we see the result. I do not think the Prime Minister would wish to have a result of that kind, I would ask him whether we may expect these grievances to be remedied and what action the Government will take.
I want further to call the attention of the Minister of Railways to the fact that last autumn, in Christmas week I think, about one-third of the trackmen were discharged, temporarily, as I understand it. At all events, one of the permanent men from each section of the road was discharged. That was a cruel thing to do right at the beginning of winter. The wages received by these men is barely sufficient to support themselves and their families, and yet right in the beginning of winter, in Christmas week, the Government dismissed them for the winter season. The men could not get any other work at that season of the year. From what I know of the Minister of Railways, I do not think that personally he would approve of conduct of that kind, but, nevertheless, his department did it. Possibly the man responsible for that is the General Manager, who is receiving a princely salary, I understand $20,000 a year. That man is in a position in which he is not obliged to feel the necessities of men who are earning a bare living wage of from $1.50 to $1.70 per day. Why, if you had a horse which had served you faithfully during the summer season, you would not turn him out at the beginning of winter to starve; if you did you would be put in prison at the instance of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to animals. I repeat that I do not think the Minister of Railways would personally do a thing like that, but being the head of the department he must be held responsible. I would now ask the Minister what redress these poor men are going to get. So serious was the matter that the trackmen held a meeting amongst themselves, and the men who had not been discharged agreed to work only alternate weeks so that they would thus share their wages with the men who were thrown out of employment. They knew thier comrades could not support their families during the winter months. That is a condition of things that is quite serious. Now, will the Minister of Railways take steps to reinstate these men, and to prevent the issuing of an order of that kind in future? I believe that personally his better nature would prompt him to take action of that kind.

I also wish to ask whether we may expect any redress so far as decrease in rates- which are excessive and which were certainly not contemplated-on the Prince Edward Island Railway. I am satisfied that if the present Prime Minister, when he went before the people of Prince Edward Island previous to the last general election, had told the people that if he were placed in office he would raise the rates on the Prince Edward Island railway to the extent they have been raised, he would have received very few votes indeed in that province.
I wish that the minister would give me an answer on these points.

As to the raising of
the rates, the increase has taken place just as on the main line of the Intercolonial railway. I may say, however, that before I came into office, and continuously for a long time, there has been a deficit on the Prince Edward Island railway, and that deficit is still about $100,000 a year.
And it always will be so.
I suppose it will.

The very necessities
of the case make it inevitable.

The hon. gentleman
(Mr. Hughes) did not say that we had raised the men's wages about 25 per cent since we came into power. It is to be remembered also that all kinds of materials have increased in price, and consequently it costs a great deal more to run now than it did a few years ago. Instructions were given to the officials at Moncton six months ago that if hardship arose in regard to any item they must inquire into the matter. According to the statement the hon. gentleman quoted he could haul wood five miles, as I understand him for $7 a car. I can only say that that rate is cheaper than it can be done in any other place in Canada that I know of. I am confident it is not the usual rate. With reference to the laying off of section men, I know that has been a hardship. But all other railways do it, and I do not know why a government railway should not be run like other railways, in a business way. If we are to continue to support government ownership and operation, we must have the ordinary business course of management.
Then no redress need be expected?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not know that that question has absolutely to be determined excepting in so far as it might be determined by the selection of some other site, than the one	suggested.	As I
have said, the Government has discontinued negotiations with regard to the acquisition of -any site. While representations have been made to the Government, as well as to hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House, -setting forth the advantages of the scheme to which reference has been made, the Government has taken no action whatever with reference to that

scheme. If any -action is taken in that regard, we will, of course, communicate our position to the House during the session, at the earliest possible moment.

I may be out of order in bringing this matter up, but it is well known that the late High Commissioner discharged the duties of his office with very great credit to himself and to Canada, and was able to do so only because of having large private means. Now that the Government is faced with the necessity of selecting a successor, the question Of the financial circumstances of the possible successor may come under consideration. I do not know that I will be warranted in asking the Government if they have decided upon any change of policy as to the amount of remuneration granted to the High Commissioner-that is if they have felt that the remuneration should be on a basis that would enable a man without fortune to occupy the position or if they have decided to leave it as at present so that the post can be filled only by a person having large private means.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think my hon. friend's question is a very proper one, and the subject which he mentions is one proper for the consideration of the Government. Up to the present time it never has been formally considered by the Government, although doubtless in the minds of the members of the Government as well as in the minds of hon. gentlemen in this House generally there has been the knowledge that some addition would require to be made to the salary, unless we are to be restricted to the appointment of persons possessed of very great private means. The subject will have to receive consideration by reason of the vacancy which has taken place through the lamented death of Lord Strathcona, and it will receive consideration.

I noticed a despatch the other day in nearly all the Government organs saying that Lord Strathcona, near the close of his life, had made a suggestion that the Hon. Adam Beck should be his successor. Have the Government heard anything of that ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not aware that Lord Strathcona made any suggestion to 4 p.m. the Government with regard to the subject.
The Government, of course, would not take my advice.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Do not be too sure.

But it might be good
nevertheless. There is no question but that the late High Commissioner was a credit to himself and to all concerned, and it would be very difficult, practically impossible, to fill his position in every respect. We in Canada are advancing now to a higher status than we have ever had before; our business interests are greater than they have ever been, and are rapidly developing. My own view is-and I have no particular individual in mind-that the Government would be well advised to select an active man for that position who knows Canada and Canadian affairs generally. It would be a great mistake to select a man who is not in close touch p with Canadian affairs, merely as a recognition of past services or anything else. The interests are too great to be trifled with, and I think it would be wise for the Government to consider carefully the selection of such a man as I have spoken of; but at all events they should not consider the appointment of any man who is not in close touch with Canadian affairs. Such a man could be of great assistance both to the empire and to this Dominion in that position.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: At pages 30 and 31 there are the details of several votes for the Commission of Conservation and the Civil Service Commission.
Could my right hon. friend give us the names of the officers of the Conservation Commission ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If my hon. friend desires that information I shall ask that the item be not taken up.

Is the Government satisfied that there is justification for the rapid increase in the cost of administering this commission ? I think there is room for doubting the wisdom of the wide latitude given this commission in the many matters in which they are supposed to take an interest. For instance, a publication was issued the other day in reference to oyster culture. Their investigations and the publication of that book alone would mean the expenditure of a considerable sum of money. At the same time the Department of Marine and Fisheries are naturally specially charged with the administration of all fisheries, and I know they have devoted considerable time and made considerable expenditure of money of late years particularly in connection with oyster culture. This is one instance of overlapping of work between
the Conservation Commission and one of the departments of government, and I think there are other illustrations of this.
I have not given very much consideration to the matter, but I think it is worthy of a little consideration and investigation by the Government whether or not the Conservation Commission are infringing upon the duties of some of the departments of government. I think further that it is worth while considering whether, after all, the services done to the country by the commission are worth its cost or whether the same services could not be as well administered by some other department of government. I recognize the fact that the commission have performed some service to the State, and the crusading work having been completed, it may be that the work can be better performed by other departments of government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would not care to enter upon the discussion without better preparation than I have at the moment. Some question was raised about this item, either last session or the session before. On that occasion I procured the very fullest information as to the work which the Commission had performed, and placeditupon'Hansard.' On that occasion also, the Committee listened to a very instructive speech from the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland), who is a member of the Conservation Commission and thoroughly familiar with his work. I supported the appointment of a Conservation Commission and the legislation by which it was constituted, believing it would be of great service to the country, and I have no reason to change the views I then entertained. It is quite possible there may be some overlapping of work; that is to be avoided as far as possible, and I would like to remind my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) that overlapping of work sometimes occurs even between different departments of the Government. Therefore, the mere transference of the work of this Commission to a department of the Government would not remedy the overlapping of which he complains. If my hon. friend would let the item stand, I will give him full information as to the work.

The Commission was appointed some four years ago on the model of the Commission appointed in the United States, and so far we have every reason for believing that the work done by the Commission has been extremely useful. They have gone very far in many directions

and particularly in one direction. I say the work which is being done by the Conservation Commission in regard to forestry is beyond praise. Last year there were less fires, at all events in the southern part of Ontario and in parts of Quebec, than in any previous year, and this is largely attributable to the efforts of the Commission. If the Commission had done nothing more than that, it would have more than justified its existence. The Chairman of the Commission, Hon. Clifford Sifton, is a very able man, and I do not think a more competent man could be found for the work. I do not know what the Commission have achieved in other directions, such as tuberculosis, but with regard to the conservation of forests I cannot for my part sufficiently emphasize my appreciation of what they have done. There is no subject of greater importance at the present time, especially in the southern parts of Ontario and Quebec, and if the Commission were to do nothing more than to teach the people the importance of this matter, I repeat they would more than justify their existence. I have taken but a cursory view of the Estimates, but I have not found any appropriation this year for a Forestry Congress. From time to time forestry associations have met in British Columbia and in Quebec, and in bringing to the attention of the people the great necessity of forest preservation have largely justified the small expenditure they involved, and I would suggest to my right hon. friend to put in an appropriation in the forthcoming Estimates for a forestry congress.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I entirely concur in the appreciation which my right hon. friend has expressed of the work of the Conservation Commission, in the prevention of forest fires. In one way and another, I have been brought into touch with their work in that regard, and it is not too much to say that the saving which they have effected to the material wealth of the country in that regard would pay all the expenses of the Commission, not only ten but a hundred times over. So far as the proposal to hold the forestry congress is concerned, I should be very glad indeed to take into consideration the suggestion which the right hon. gentleman has made.
If I remember correctly there was one held about two years ago, in British Columbia, I think.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: But not here.
That was an association, not a Government affair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: At all events I shall look into the matter and give consideration to what my right hon. friend has suggested.

Might I be allowed to
give a concrete case of the good work done by this commission-a case where they were useful to at least one department of the Government. It is true they may overlap but I am not sure that that is to the detriment of the public. When the question of protecting forests along the lines of railway came up, there was very strong objection on the part of railways to legislation that was being discussed at that time by private members in the House. As it was a very serious grievance, I called together on one occasion, one or two men who are deeply interested in the protection of forests, as individuals, two representatives of the railways and two of the representatives of the Conservation Commission including the Chairman, I think, and one other, and before they separated they handed me a draft section for the amendment to the Railway Act. It was acceptable to the railways and to the lumbermen and is now part of the Railway Act, and of great benefit I am told. Had it not been for the Conservation Commission, I am afraid we should not have been able to come to such a satisfactory conclusion. Although I would like to know the names of the officers for one or two reasons that I may discuss later on, I am strongly in favour of the work of the commission and if they do occasionally make mistakes, I have known even Governments to do that.

The answer which the
Government made to the application of the city of Ottawa involved as its first condition, an abundant supply of pure water. Up to the present time, the city has never been able to come to us and say they are ready to proceed with a certain proposal. When they do come to us with the assurance that they will be able to carry out a certain proposal, we will avail ourselves of the technical assistance of the officers of the Conservation Commission as well as all other necessary technical assistance, in order that we may be sure the country is not spending its money on an imperfect or poor supply. Up to the present day I have not had occasion to ask the assistance of the officers of the commission in that regard.
Civil Service Commission-Commissioners' salaries, $15,000.

This is a department
which comes, I think, under the administration of my hon. friend the Secretary of State. I do not see him present, and we require some information which perhaps my right hon. friend would not have in his possession.

Civil Government-Department of Trade and Commerce, $103,237.50.

What is the occasion of the increase over last year?
Hon. GEORGE E. FOSTER (Minister of Trade and Commerce):	Speaking generally, there is nothing but the statutory increases. Then, specially, there is an increase of one in the first division, subdivision A and of two in the first division, subdivision B, making the number of increases three in the whole. That is for the Department of Trade and Commerce proper. In the Census and Statistics branch there is provision made for three at the minimum in the third division, subdivision A, because in the arrangement for the statistical work of the department for next year we shall need to have some more help in the way of stenographers and clerks.
Going back to the Department of Trade and Commerce, we are making provision for the establishment of the grain laboratory in connection with the grain work of the department. In the United States they have of late been paying a great deal of attention to the more scientific investigation of grain
as regards the qualities of grain, the moisture contents and problems that arise in storage and transportation, with the idea of getting at a scientific basis for coming to better conclusions as to the management of the grain itself and also as to the value of grain distributed under the different standards. It seemed to me that some such work as that ought to be undertaken as soon as possible in Canada where we have so large an output of grain at present with almost illimitable possibilities for the increase of the output. Our grain production is going to be one of the great productions of the future, and we need as good scientific knowledge as we can get in reference to it, as well as good distributive and administrative knowledge in the practical working out of the Grain Act. The Grain Commissioners took up the matter, and after a pretty thorough investigation they made a report recommending the establishment of a laboratory. We propose to start it with two chemists, one an over chemist who is the real grain chemist, and the other whose duty shall be more in reference to arriving at the values of grain as regards milling, baking and bread-making properties. It is proposed to establish this at Winnipeg, and to conduct tests there mainly. We shall have to get accommodation, which is now being arranged for, and a certain amount of laboratory material will be necessary to enable the chemists to carry on their investigations and make their experiments. In connection with that, as the work goes on, there will be a deeper and more thorough experimentation and analysis required which will necessitate larger means at the disposal of the chemist in the shape of laboratory facilities to enable him to thoroughly carry these investigations out. It is proposed to accomplish that part of the work in affiliation and co-operation with the laboratories either in Montreal or in Toronto in connection with the universities. That will be for taking certain matters up and submitting them to laboratory tests of a rather delicate and thorough nature. It would be too costly for us to equip the laboratory at Winnipeg to enable the chemist to carry on that work.
The board were instructed to make inquiries and to get information as to the proper officials for this and as a result they recommended the appointment of Dr. Birchard, who had a distinguished course in the University at Toronto and who since then has been employed in Washington in the prosecution of this kind of work under the Government there.

and in the Government laboratories of the United States there. He has, as I have said, had a distinguished career and his qualifications seem to be of a very high character and such as would indicate him to be a man thoroughly qualified to carry on that work. Then, in regard to the other side of the work, which, in one sense, is the more practical, or at least has the more practical side to it, we had to arrange and after a good deal of search we hoped to be able to get a man from the University at Minneapolis who has been engaged in that kind of work for the State authorities there, but we were not able to do that. In the end we have been able to get a man who has been connected with the same kind of work under the Government of the United States at Washington and he was recommended to us by the authorities as being as good a man as can be obtained in the United-States for this work.
These two will form the staff as far as the scientific part of it is concerned. A stenographer and a clerk, the two combined in one, will do the rest of the work that is necessary and a moderate supply of laboratory equipment will furnish them with what is necessary for carrying on their work. The head chemist is already at work and naturally his duties fell in with the general work of the administration of the Act, but after considering the matter it seemed to me that the staff equipment of the laboratory for carrying on this investigation might well be provided by the Government from the general fund and that we might thus relieve the fund which arises from the imposition of fees upon the grain that passes inspection and leave that free from this part of the work. Therefore, I introduce it here, and I would like the committee to give the necessary authority for the employment of these chemists, and vote the necessary sum so that at the beginning oi the fiscal year these officials shall be a charge upon the general consolidated fund.
Was it impossible to get competent officials in Canada?

We have had practically
no experimental work of that kind in Canada, and in the inception of the work you can only get your expert men from places where they have had training and experience. We could not find these men in Canada just at this time. But our chemist is a Canadian by birth and education, and his family live in Canada.
But the other one?
I do not think it is best, at the inception of this, to take men without experience and without training, because we want to start in the very best possible way.
I agree with that.
Have not experiments been carried on at the Experimental Farm at Ottawa, in reference to the milling qualities of wheat?

Such experiments may
have been carried on in a very casual way. What the experimental farms are chiefly after, is, to get a variety of grain which as a seed will have good qualities and will ripen as early as possible.
Are the duties of the Commissioner of Commerce superior to those of the Deputy Minister of the Department; I see he is paid a higher salary than the deputy minister.

It sometimes happens that a salary is paid to -a man in the service which may be higher than the salary paid to another man, who, in certain respects, has wider duties and greater responsibilities. The deputy minister is the sole deputy minister of the department. The Commissioner of Commerce is an official with special qualifications and special experience, and I was able to get his services from the British Government for the special purpose for which I desired them, and I paid him exactly the same salary as he was being paid by the Colonial Office for the work he was carrying on as British Trade Commissioner in Canada.
What is he supposed to do?

The Commissioner of
Commerce, under the direction of the minister, has to pay special attention to the commercial exchanges, their source, their destination, and the process of interchange.
I placed under his personal supervision our trade commissionerships in different parts of the world, and all our transactions with the British consular service in so far as they relate to trade and commerce. I am not saying anything as to the previous work done in -the department, but any minister who has had charge of a department knows that the work of a deputy minister must extend over every part of the department. He has to be general supervisor of everything, and it is not possible for a deputy minister who has a

large department to spend too much time on any one service. This service was, in my belief, of sufficient importance to have direct supervision, and a directing officer, in order to get from the expenditure of a large amount of money, something like the return we ought to have. I am not at all satisfied we .are getting all the return we ought to get from the trade commission-erships at the present time, but we are improving that service. One of the most -effective ways of improving it is to have that service understand that there is some man who is especially charged with seeing that the work is being carried on properly.
I have had the Commissioner of Commerce visit all the trade commissionerships in Europe, and China and Japan. I was fortunate enough to be able to look in upon them in Australia and New Zealand, so that during the past year we did, what was never done before, and which I am sure every one will admit ought to be done. The change has resulted in the very best influence, and I purpose that every year in some way or other an officer from the head department shall get into communication in the locality with the trade commissioners, and in that way come to a better appreciation of the work that is *being done and that is to be done.
Another very important part of the work, and which I think has been neglected in the past, is, that after we had been successful in getting valuable information from the outside, a great deal of that information has not been able to penetrate to the points in Canada where it might come into contact with those whom it would benefit. It is one thing to gather good information; it is another thing to see that information properly and wide y distributed. It is the design of the department to make that information thoroughly available and to distribute it more widely than in the past. Then the man who is outside, in order to do good work on the outside, must occasionally refresh himself at the fountainhead, and I am not sure but what, taking year in and year out, three months or so spent by one of our trade commissioners from abroad in Canada interviewing the men with whom he has had a good deal of correspondence in the course of the year, would be a good thing for the service.

This is not
going to be one of these commissions whose reports are shelved?
It is very unkind to make that remark at the present time when I am serious.

In my judgment the appointment of the trade commissi n:r is a good idea, as is also the bringing of the commissioners home to interview those in Canada who have trade with foreign countries. I do not understand yet, ho \ ever, how the deputy minister, who is over the whole department, should get less salary than the man who is in charge tnly of: a branch of the department. I would like to know how the producer in the West can be benefited by the work of the gram chemist?
As a general proposition, the producer will get the most benefit in proportion as he has larg.r knowledge with reference to the article he produces.

I refei to the ordinary
farmer.

If these officers can come to correct and scientific conclusions as, for example, to the moisture in grain and how it affects storage and transport and get it down to the point where it will be made as safe as it possibly can be made, that will have the effect of standardizing conditions under which grain may be marketed, and stored and transported, end the producer, of course, will benefit from that.

How does the minister
propose to distribute that knowledge?

That will be distributed
broadcast through our bulletins and the newspapers. One looking at the number of bulletins distributed every week would be apt to say that it bore a very small proportion to the number of people who ought to be reached. But I have had that matter particularly followed, and I find the bulletin is multiplied a thousand, perhaps ten thousand, times by reproduction in the newspapers of pertinent information contained in these bulletins. 1 am trying to get the trade commissioners to appreciate what it is the most important for our people here to know and to put that into pithy and luminous reports. These reports are given in the bulletins, and when you get such matter into the bulletins, the newspapers do not have to be solicited to put it into their columns. It is very gratifying to see the number of extracts made from our bulletins and given wide circulation in the newspapers throughout the Dominion. The processes discovered by these chemists

will be published in bulletin form and distributed as widely as possible.

Speaking of trade agents, has Mr. Poindron of the Paris office been replaced? He has been removed, I do not know whether by death or resignation, and I believe there is no trade agent there now. Am I correct in that?

No, my hon. friend is not correct, if he says there is no trade commissioner there. When I came into the department, I found a double-headed arrangement in Paris. At the head of one part was a commissioner, and at the head of another, Mr. Poindon. It became possible to do eway with one section of it, and the trade commissioner in Paris now is Mr. Roy. Mr. Roy is not in any sense one who represents Canada in a diplomatic or financial way. He is charged with the trade commissioner's work and is doing that work. It would not be fair, and it would not be correct, to say that we have no trade commissioner in Paris. The business of the trade commissionership is being done by Mr. Roy and very much more effectively than when I took charge of the department.

I know Mr. Roy to be
highly competent in his work, and I know he has given Canada great satisfaction. But I did not think it possible in France to have the commissioner general act as trade agent when in other countries there are several trade agents. That is why I asked the question.

There is not in any sense a separate form of agency in France any more than in other countries. Mr. Roy does in Paris what the trade commissioner does in Australia. He is the commissioner and represents Canada. All questions regarding trade are directed to him, and the answers so far as he can give them are sent from his office. He also carries on communications with inquirers, and for any information that he has not, he applies to us. The whole modus operandi, so far as the trade commissionership is concerned, is in full operation between this department, Mr. Roy and inquirers in France.
And the minister may fairly claim that he has made a necessary economy ?

I did not see that it was necessary to have two separate establish-
ments doing the same business and quarrelling with each other while doing it.

The minister has
spoken about the distribution of information obtained by his department. He deals first with the bulletins. Can he tell us through what means and to what persons and bodies these bulletins are sent ? In my own city of Saskatoon I have never seen the bulletin except as I receive it as a member of Parliament. It may be that the board of trade receives it, also the university library, and the public library, and others. If they do not, I would suggest that these are very popular bodies to be in receipt of the bulletin. Perhaps the hon. minister could tell us what rule is followed in regard to that.

What we have to guard against is the sending of bulletins to persons where they simply become material for feeding wastepaper baskets. We want to get the bulletin into the hands of those who will really appreciate it. So, there has been a good deal of sifting in that respect. All boards of trade get the bulletin, and all boards of trade are notified that if any member of the board or any person in the trade would like to have the bulletin sent regularly, he has only to send in his name. We have advertised also quite widely in that direction to get people to tell us who would like to receive the bulletin. When we send to such people we have the best ground possible for believing that they are utilizing it and getting some good from it. Not only boards of trade, but associations and public bodies of all kinds connected with trade are being made aware that we are trying to get the bulletin into the hands of those who would like to read it and file it as a means of information. Perhaps I ought not to pass an opinion on it, but I think I am right in saying that any one who will read the bulletin from week to week will find it very useful and well worth filing and keeping for reference. Last year, Mr. Poussette, our trade commissioner in South America, who is a very efficient man, acting under my instructions, made a tour of South America, visiting every one of the constituted governmental divisions, making inquiries and examinations into trade conditions, products, resources and the possibilities of interchange of goods with Canada. Mr. Poussette embodied his in-

vestigations in reports which have been published in the bulletin, and I think that any person who has had the pleasure of reading them appreciates the information given.

Early last year it was announced that my hon. friend was extending the work of his department by opening up an agency or agencies in South Africa. Is tha+ work under the supervision of the Commissioner of Commerce, and how has it resulted?

Yes, it is in charge of the Commissioner of Commerce. Our former trade commissioner in South Africa is no longer in the work, and I transferred to that office one of the most efficient trade commissioners in Great Britain, Mr. Egan, who, I think, came originally from Montreal. Mr. Egan has taken charge of our interests in South Africa, and, I must say, is conducting a most energetic canvas of the country. His principal office is in Cape Town. I have had him make a tour of Sputh Africa, and we are establishing in five or six different places a correspondent, in each case a resident, who will work under the instructions of the Commissioner, answering all inquiries, and keeping the Commissioner generally posted with reference to trade requirements at these points. These officials are contributories to the information that Mr. Egan must himself gather, and which he reports to the Department. The system is, I think, a good one, and is working well. Once or twice a year Mr. Egan makes a tour of the country and consults with the correspondents. The correspondents work at a smaller salary, not devoting all their time to the work, but, by means of a judicious selection of men at each point, an official is generally obtained who is capable of doing the work, first because he has a tendency and a liking for the work; secondly, because it is a somewhat honorary position, and thirdly because he is doing a good service for both countries. The enlargement of trade with South Africa during the last year, so far as our exports are concerned, has been very satisfactory.
What will be the total cost of the chemistry office in Winnipeg?

The fittings of the laboratory office will not be expensive or palatial.
We have a couple of rooms which have to be fitted up with special plumbing and the necessary laboratory material. There will be the cost of installation and the rental, services of a clerk and stenographer-one official will be necessary to do this work- and other expenses will run up to somewhere about $6,000 or $7,000 a year.

Are the trade representatives doing any practical work in the way of putting the people in touch with business men in this country? I understand that the commercial agents of the United States in foreign countries very often succeed in bringing orders to the business men of the United States by letting them know what is required in the places where they happen to be. For example, if a railroad were being built in Australia, would your commercial agent, if he discovered that 2,000 tons of steel rails were required in the construction of that railway, endeavour to put the contractors in touch with the steel people of Canada? Do they do practical work of that kind, or do they simply collect information and submit it to the department in the form of a bulletin?

They are supposed so to
keep their eyes open that not a single transaction of that kind will escape their notice. Their duties do not consist of merely sitting in their offices and gathering statistical information. The official statistical information is good, but it is the smallest part of the information that a trade commissioner ought to be able to furnish the department. We have trade commissioners and trade commissioners; of course you have to have a man who is wide-awake, and who likes to work rather than sit in his office. I could name a good many of these commissioners who are doing invaluable work.
Referring to the example I cited to the hon. minister, how would the necessary information reach the manufacturer of steel rails in Canada?

In the first place, the trade commissioner keeps himself alive to what is going on, say in New Zealand. He sees the New Zealand papers; he has access to Government and official information, and if he is alive to his work he knows in a general way, what is going on in every department of the Government. He knows also

what is going on so far as general expansion, improvement and development of the country is concerned; he knows what is going on in the way of railway and power development. When machinery, for instance, is required, he presents to those concerned the possibilities of satisfying their wants in this or any other respect in Canada. He puts them in direct connection with the department here, and so with the manufacturers or producers of the articles which they may require. That is the general modus operandi.

In connection with the
information which the hon. minister was good enough to give the committee with regard to the new grain department at Winnipeg, may I ask him if it is open to the general public to avail themselves of the services of these experts, or will these gentlemen perform only such services as they are directed by the department to perform? Would they make tests at the request of the grain growers, for instance, the same as would be done at the experimental farm?

Their main object will be to take up, analyse and experiment upon grain, and the result arrived at will be published and become the property of everybody. In so far as that is concerned, they are doing a general service, and the results will be for general use. For instance, suppose some new kind of grain, thought to be of good quality, has been raised in some part of the West, it would be the duty of that department to look into that, to analyse it, find out its qualities and in that way they would be abie to advertise to the producing public the different kinds of grain of largest value and therefore the best to be raised by the producer in order to get better value and better results. We have to take'care to guard against making it a dribbling office which will fritter away its time on requests, here, there and everywhere. It must keep in view the main object. If any result should come from it it must be a practical result in the end because that is the whole design of the formation of the commission.
If an individual farmer had a new kind of grain he would be allowed to send it to this commission to be -analysed and then the result would be made public.

It seems to me that that is the most feasible and important thing the agents can do, to show what trade can be done between this and other countries by getting in actual personal contact with the manufacturers of this country.

In regard to the increase in the Census Branch, what is
5 p.m. the particular occasion for the extension next year?

My hon. friend will recollect that we appointed a departmental commission on statistics and that commission reported last year. Gradually we are strengthening in my department the statistical side. Since I took office I have gone along very slowly, I have made no additions to the working staff particularly,

and I find it is necessary, in order to carry out the work of the department, that we *should have more of what might be called secondary help, and we must have the money to pay them.
Is the hon. gentleman endeavouring to secure statistical data respecting interprovincial trade? I remember that when in opposition he always urged the necessity of this and quite properly so.

I have given this matter a great deal of consideration. As a principle it is a very fine idea, if we could only know just exactly the currents of trade between the different sections of our own country in different products according to sectional and seasonal differences it would give us a great insight into the trade and producing activities of our country. When you come to work out a plan by which that information can be secured you encounter difficulties on every side.

Did the minister ever
try to make any arrangement with the provincial governments to secure this?

When the report was published I sent it to all the provincial governments and also a letter calling attention to the overlapping of statistics between the Dominion and the provinces and asking their attention and that of their statistical officers to the matter to see whether we could not amongst us devise a system which would co-relate the work better, provide against overlapping and produce accuracy. [DOT] All of the provincial governments took the matter up in a friendly and kindly spirit and after that I had the Commissioner of Commerce visit all the provincial capitals and get into personal communication with the statistical officers. That has been done, and while nothing has yet eventuated in a plan, yet we have made substantial progress in the general improvement of our statistics in these two ways, by a co-relation of effort, preventing overlapping and in consequence securing greater accuracy. If we could only get fresher statistics of production in this country it would be of great benefit and I hope there is a way by which we can do this.

How long is it since
the statistical work was taken over by the Department of Trade and Commerce from the Department of Agriculture?
About a year.

It seems to me to be a time when the hands of the minister should be held up in connection with the trade agencies in these various countries. I have not heard him say whether it is the policy of the department to extend this system to other countries not yet covered. In Brantford we have several firms doing business with twelve or fifteen foreign countries at the present time. In some of these countries we have no trade agents. I think there is not one in Russia.
No.

A very large trade is being done from Brantford with Russia. A large trade is being done with some South American republics and with South Africa. I think we have an agent appointed there. I have been a frequenter of some of the offices, having visited Australia not long ago. I then had an opportunity of seeing what is going on there and I must say that the agent in charge, Mr. Ross, was doing very fine work. They have a good office but not too good and I think this House might well be liberal with any appointments the minister might ask with a view to increasing our trade with foreign countries. At the present time, trade is sought very keenly by all the great countries in the world. Canada is comparatively small but has great possibilities, and I think the Minister is doing excellent work and should be encouraged to establish trade agencies in countries where there are none already. It will be easier to get a footing now in those countries than later on, and I would like to suggest to the hon. Minister that if we can establish in the coming year say two or three agencies in the different countries with which we have a large trade, we should do a still larger business with them if our case was presented to the people of those countries. I am speaking of Canadian products, generally, not -manufactured articles only. I think it would be of great advantage to open up trade with some of these countries in such goods as we have a surplus of. I wish to speak a word of encouragement to the Minister in this respect. I think he is making his department a real live business affair which is appreciated by business men all over the country. I think an agency should be established at London. An agency there would be an advertisement to the whole world, because people who never come to Canada do visit London, and they could see our products there. With this and a real live trade Commissioner in the heart of the empire, I believe the overseas

trade of the Dominions could be vastly increased in the next few years. It is a trade that is well worth looking after, and now that Canada is beginning to do business in foreign countries I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce should be liberally dealt with in anything he may ask for, either with regard to agencies already established, or proposed agencies. With regard to the dissemination of information I, myself, receive the bulletins regularly. I do not know whether they reach the hands of some people who want them, but I think that any firm sending a request to Ottawa for these bulletins should be obliged in that respect. I do not think it would be wise that the Minister should become, or that his agent should become, the agent of any individual firm, that would lead to confusion. The aim should be to bring together those who have goods for sale and those who want to buy. As has been mentioned by one gentleman opposite, the United States make a very great effort in the direction of having their agents act for one particular firm. They have very live consular agents, who	act	as trade
agents as well, and the spread of United States trade over the world * has been largely brought about by the men they have sent out, and who are always ready to draw attention to the trade that may be developed in foreign countries. I think we can take a leaf out of their book, although I am not favourable to copying the United States in a great many things. I just rose to say these few words in appreciation. The strengthening and information we get through these trade agencies is very helpful to the spread of trade, at least so far as our district is concerned.
I do not know that anybody on this side of the House has been criticising the Minister. We were asking for information.	i

I did not speak in
that sense at all.
We were asking for information, and I suppose we have a right to that.
So far as I was concerned I had no fault to find with any-that has been asked for or said.

It is so seldom the opportunity occurs on which I can agree with my hon. friend, that I take this opportunity of agreeing with him as to the entire desirability of pushing Canadian
[Mr. Cockshutt 1
trade in all her products, whether of the field, the forest, the mine or the factory; and so far as the Minister of Trade and Commerce is minded to direct the efforts of the Government to that end, I am sure he has had evidence here to-day, that although it is our business on this side to criticise, we are also willing to commend where commendation is possible.

If I am not boring the
Committee, I would like to say one or two things. In the first place, with reference to commercial agents and trade commissioners working for special firms, they do not do that at all. They cannot be allowed to do it. Trade commissioners are not supposed, and ought never to be supposed, to be the agents of any particular or special firms. I want to mention another thing, especially to my hon. friend here and such men as he, that no matter how much trade agencies and oommis-sionerships may be perfected, there is nothing in the wide world will do what, a manufacturer or producer fails to do for himself outside of all this which is merely helpful. The man who wants to push his trade in a foreign country has to go there himself or send his representative to put his wares before the faces of the people, and talk with them. One of the faults that we have to overcome in our country to-day is this; we do not find our commercial and manufacturing concerns and our producing concerns, in comparison with some other very live countries, pushing their trade in the world. We have not the capable, persistent, uniform representation of goods that we ought to have. Our commissioners, who work some of them very hard and after a length of time get into communication with a man who wants something in another country and the man who can provide it here, and perhaps actually get the orders find that the man here when he receives the order is lax about even answering the correspondence; or having accepted the order he delays in filling it. Or, still further, having accepted an order, after a length of time he writes to his correspondent that he is too full of business here and that he cannot fill the order.
The hon. minister does not find that generally?

More generally than 1 would like to find it. And it does tw'o things: it takes the vim out of the commissioner himself, who has spent a great deal of valuable time in order to make the connection, and it leads the prospective

customer to say: ' Well, I cannot do business with that man; I have riven him an order, and now he writes me that he is too full of business, and cannot fill it?5 I -wanted to speak about that, not in the way of fault-finding, but as something we should make progress in. Another point I might mention is this:	My friend here spoke
about trade commissioners in foreign countries with which we do more or less business. We have always had a friendly feeling towards Canada and Canadian trade amongst the commercial intelligence officers of Great Britain in their different consulates in different parts of the world. Most of them have been favourably disposed towards Canada and willing to answer questions and to assist us in our trade. But it never was on a basis before where each consulate felt that they were carrying out what the foreign and colonial offices wanted them to carry out in that respect. An arrangement was made, without any great difficulty and very satisfactorily, with the Colonial Office and Foreign Office by which instructions have been given to the British consuls in foreign countries that they are to adopt a certain course in any case where the Canadian department feels that there is some possibility of developing trade for Canada. Instructions have been issued by the Foreign Office to British consuls in these countries, and they may include any country where an application is made by Canada to have such done, that they are to do certain things; in the first place, to forward copies of their general reports to the Department of Trade and Commerce here; secondly, to answer any inquiries from Canadian merchants or traders that are made to them in reference to the possibilities of trade or any question that might come up between a person here and a possible trade opportunity in another country. Under these instructions they will feel that they have a warrant for doing what they did in many cases before of their own good will and of their own good will only. We have made further arrangement and it is this: Go into a country like Russia, which is surrounded by some difficulties in pushing trade from another country, official or otherwise, or go to China and you have established there old and experienced British consulates with intelligent and experienced commercial men attached to them. I am thinking of one now in the far East where I met some of the brightest commercial men whom I have ever met, who have had from fifteen to twenty years of experience in these countries, who know all the 21}
ins and outs and customs of the trade, and *particularly -the things that have to be *done in order to get trade and how to * approach people. They have had all that experience.
We have made arrangement whereby it is possible that a room shall be provided under the roof of the consulate in which the Canadian commissioner may be placed, for which room, the Canadian Government although the British Foreign Office did not wish it at all, will pay the expenses and charges. I thought it better to do that in order that we should be perfectly independent in that respect than to ask the British consulate to take upon themselves the expense of the rental. Our own trade commissioner will be absolutely under the control of the department. He will take his instructions from here and do his work under these instructions, but at the same time he will have as ready friends and helpers men of wide and large experience right at his elbow from whom he can ask advice and counsel and from whom he can get what is so invaluable-knowledge which has been gained by many years of experience. In some cases I am arranging to place men under these conditions and the British Foreign Office have gone so far as to say that they are willing to open up the consular service to young men from Canada just the same as to young men from the British Islands. In this way we get two things; we get first the value of the co-operation, experience and advice of experienced men and in the other case we are able to look forward to the time not far distant when the Canadian trade commissioner system 3hall be somewhat of a career which shall approve itself to men and which shall induce young men to fit themselves by a proper course of study to undertake this work. If they do that they have not only this position in the Canadian trade com-missionership system to look forward to but, if they wish it, they have also a chance for entrance into the wider British commercial system as well. I talked that matter over in China and Japan with the British Ambassadors and both of them are absolutely enthusiastic in joining in an endeavour of that kind. They say that a capable representative of Canada at1 their side is of as much use to them in one way as would be a member of their own consulate because he is able to give them just the information that they require in reference to a country with which in China, Japan and other countries the British Consul has a great deal to do m other matters.

Allusion was made to the consular system of the United States. It-is not so many years ago, that, I think I may say without saying anything that is not -right, the trade consular system of the United States was not a thing that United States people were proud of. From every quarter there were comments and criticisms and very sharp ones of that service. At that time it was absolutely a matter of patronage. To-day the United States consular system is placed on a stated civil service basis. Men must be approved before they enter it and then when they go into service it has its status, its permanency and also its wider horizon. To-day the United States consular service is a service that the people of the United States may very well be proud of.

Is the trade service of
Canada on a permanent civil service basis?

It is not on a civil service basis theoretically but I intend before ioftg to ask the House to put it upon a permanent basis. My views, when I came into office, of the possibilities and mechanism of that work were somewhat different from what they are now. The two years in which I have had experience of it has been a period in which I have been trying to find out what is the best system.
Will the young men that the minister speaks of be required to speak and understand the language of these foreign countries before they receive their appointments?
That depends. Of course in reference to British countries they have the language already.
But in foreign countries?

In reference* to foreign
countries, I should like to have, for instance in Japan, a man sufficiently young and sufficiently well trained as a basis and with sufficient vim in him to say to himself. I will acquire the Japanese language before I am long in this country and I will learn to speak the language that the people speak, try to think what the people think and try to enter into the true spirit andigenius of the people. You have to carry that out as best you can; in some cases it can be done and in others it cannot. There is where we get the benefit of having a commissioner in the office of the British consulate where there are men who understand Japanese, and Chinese, and Russian, and our man gets the benefit of that to some extent.

I do not wish to put my opinion against that of the minister, on the matter of doing work jointly with the British consular service, but I venture the opinion that it is possibly not the best way to advance the trade interests of Canada. Is the increase of help required in any particular branch of the statistical work or is it due generally to the expansion of trade?

It is due to the expansion of the work generally.

architect do?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is thought that a man should be engaged who has a knowledge of law. Mr. Martel when appointed was a very young man-I think he is only twenty-six years of age now. I have been informed, I do not know whether correctly or not, that the Department of Marine and Fisheries in making appointments of technical officers has not observed the Civil Service Act with regard to the qualifications required. Possibly I am not well enough informed to put the question now in a form which will entitle me to an answer from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know to what my hon. friend refers. So far as I know there has been nothing of that kind.
I will have to instruct myself more fully and ask the question later.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
When technical officers are required, we apply to the Civil Service Commission under the Act. They adverting and get applications from gentlemen who state their qualifications. As a rule, they submit to us the number whom they think qualified for the position, those to whom they are ready to grant a certificate of qualification, and from that number we make our appointments. That is the way it has been done ever since I took charge Of the department.
I wonder if I may be permitted, as the Marine Estimates are still under consideration, to refer to a statement made by my hon. friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) this afternoon. I was not in the House at the time, and I have obtained a copy of the report. The hon. gentleman read an extract from the paper to which he said he wished to call the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, which was to the effect that the steamer Alert had been pressed into the service ' to convey Tory organizer Hayes and Tory candidate McLeod from North Sydney to the northern part of Victoria county,' and further that, ' the primary object in establishing this branch of the preventive service was to put a stop to the traffic of contraband liquor into Cape Breton seaports	 Notwithstanding this, some of the barrels placed on board the Government boat on its northward journey looked uncommonly like vessels containing ordinary booze.' I do not know why the hon. gentleman called my attention to this matter, as the Alert is is no way con-
*

trolled by the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
What did the department pay for the Alert?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We did not pay anything.
Who did pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know. The article refers to the ' preventive service.' If the steamer is under the Government control at all, I should infer that it is under the Dej:>artment of Customs.
That makes it no better.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, but surely the hon. gentleman does not accept every newspaper I>aragraph as being true.

I think the hon. Minister will do me the credit of believing that I was asking for information. As this statement has been made broadcast in the press of the Maritime provinces, it should be investigated. If I made a mistake in calling it to the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, it is only because I thought all these boats were under his jurisdiction. Perhaps the Minister of Custonfs (Mr. Reid) will explain the matter?
Will the Minister of Customs promise to look into this matter tomorrow?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Customs):
speechtext:
' I had not heard of it before, and I think the
article-

It may be a case of smuggling liquor from St. Pierre Miquelon into Cape Breton. That has been done before. I think the hon. Minister should inquire into it. Will he let us know the result of his inquiry on Monday?
I will. I do not know whether this steamer belongs to the Customs Department or not. But I will make inquiry and shall be glad to give the hon. member a reply on Monday.
I desire to ask the Minister of Marine and Fisheries if the Gladiator is under his Department?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
