Civil Government-Department of Naval Service-Salaries, $107,300 ; contingencies, $37,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Last year this salary vote was $100,500. The increase is chiefly made up of statutory increases. The contingencies also show an increase in this branch, just as in the Marine and Fisheries, and for the same reason, that is that all travelling expenses are charged under the head of contingencies. Now they are divided between what is the Navy, the Hydrographic Survey, the Fishery Protection Service, the Tidal Service and the Wireless Department, all of which come under the control of the Naval Department. It is proposed to have this vote under the head of Contingencies, so that it will be seen what the travelling expenses of the department as a whole are during the year.
Is any of this money expended under the operation of the Naval Service Act of 1910?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, I fancy the bulk of it is expended under that Act. Provision is made for the appointment of an inspector in the radio-telegraphic branch, to meet the increasing work in that office. Hon. gentlemen know that during the last year a number of wireless stations were erected, and it has been found necessary to appoint an additional inspector in order that the work may be carried out with efficiency; the appointment being under subdivision A of the second division, at a minimum salary of $1,600. The other changes shown are to provide for the promotion of certain members of the staff and for statutory increases in salary. I have explained the increase in connection with contingencies; it is merely an apparent increase, as the charges for travelling will be no more than they were last year.

The vote asked for by the minister under the heading of the Naval Service is one, I think, in respect of which hon. gentlemen on this side of the

House may very well request more detailed information, and if very good reasons are not given we should refuse our assent to the voting of these moneys. There is no attempt on the part of the Government of the day to administer the Naval Service Act; on the contrary, so far as we can gather, it is their public policy to allow it to remain in abeyance. There is not a ship of the Canadian navy now in service. The Rainbow, which was stationed on the Pacific coast, has, I think, been sold.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.

At least, the Rainbow is not in active service. The Niobe has during the whole summer been tied to a wharf in Halifax harbour-a condition of affairs most humiliating, I am sure, to every respectable Canadian. I have no hesitation in saying that the Government were a party to forcing men to leave the ship Niobe, and I am sure I am correct in saying that they have never yet made an effort to complete the enlistment of that ship. Notwithstanding the fact that the Government refuses to administer the Canadian Naval Service Act and does everything it can to discourage the enlistment of men under that Act, we find that the cost of administering the naval service increases. There should be some greater justification for the request which the minister makes to Parliament for the passing of the items now before the committee. Personally I do not think that this House should give its assent to the passing of these items, which are particularly referable to the Canadian Naval Service Act. The officials of the Canadian Naval Service, for whose salaries the minister now asks the voting of money, cannot be rendering any service to Canada. It may be necessary to have in the Civil Service men to administer the fisheries protection service, the wireless telegraphy service, and the like, but I submit that there is no justification whatever for the minister's asking Parliament to vote money for the administration of a service which the Government have been taking great pains to inform the Canadian people that they do not intend to maintain, for the present at least. I was told by the minister last year that the department was not encouraging the departure of men from the ship Niobe, and that the Government were not averse to securing, if possible, further enlistments to fill the vacancies that were occurring from time to time. I was also specifically told last year, in answer to a question I put to the minister, that a programme of service was contemplated for the Niobe during the summer in the way of cruises, manoeuvres, and the like, hut judging by the actions of the department since then I am bound to say that I question the bona fides of the minister and his department in the answer that they gave to me last session in reference to this matter. I think that Parliament is entitled to a reason from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the Government before a single dollar of money is granted for the Naval Service as now requested. The minister must clearly see that to ask for a vote of practically $100,000 when there is no service to administer, is simply fooling and trifling with the Canadian public and wasting the money of the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend is, by his remarks, unintentionally giving the House a wrong impression of this matter. The hon. gentleman speaks as if he were under the impression that the money we are asking for the Naval Department of the Civil Government is all for the purpose of carrying out what may be called the work in connection with the navy.

The larger part
of it, you said a moment ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I said the smaller portion of it. The Naval Department, as I have pointed out, administers the fisheries protection service, the hydrographic survey, the wireless service, the tidal service, and certain other branches of the public service. Of these Estimates, $31,060 is for the naval portion of the service, and $76,490 is for the other branches.
Where do you put the deputy minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
One-half of the deputy
minister's salary is charged up to the naval branch and one-half to the others; this, I think, is as fair a division as may be made.

Has the cost of the marine and fisheries branch of the service decreased in the last year, or is it just as it was when the department administered the fisheries protection service and the other branches which have been mentioned?	,

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I cannot answer my hon. friend, because in order to do so I would have to go back to a time before I was Minister of Marine and Fisheries. The classification of the branches of the ser-

vice took place before the present Government came into power, and I am not familiar with the figures. The Estimates for 1911 were made by friends of the hon. gentleman; since 1911 there has been very little increase in the cost of the service, and any increases have been due to the provision for statutory increases and the appointment of new officials.

My hon.
friend knows that when the late Government determined to have a Naval Service Act and a naval service, a naval depart ment was established, and to this was attached certain of the branches of the service which were formerly attached to the Marine and Fisheries Department. We created, amongst other offices, a Deputy Minister of Naval Affairs, and. of course, in connection with this office there were secretaries and so on. If it be the intention of my hon. friend to vote for the Bill which is now before the House to repeal the Naval Service Act, what is the use of these estimates? The matter has only to be referred back to where it was. The hydrographic survey, the wireless service, and other branches referred to, have only to be restored to their original positions. But my hon. friend will apparently do neither the one nor the other. He will not carry on the Naval Act. As I understand it, he has discouraged the training of officers for the naval service and the enlistment of men. I do not know if he has maintained the Naval College, I think he has. So far so good, that is under the Naval Act. Has he sold the Rainbow or the Niobe?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.

He has kept
them without doing anything at all. They are there but have no men on them. He has made no effort to recruit men; I do not think he has even made an effort to punish men who desert the service. I do not think there has been a single prosecution for desertion; I think he has rather encouraged desertion.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.

He has not made any very strong effort to prevent it. Has he ever prosecuted a man for desertion? I know that in our little army and in the Mounted Police if a man deserts his engagement he is prosecuted as a warning to the others, but my hon. friend has closed

his eyes, has done nothing; but he still maintains the service. What answer has he therefore to the criticisms of my friends behind me? Why does he ask this appropriation if he does not want to have a naval service? If you do not want to have a naval service, just go back to the condition we were in in 1911. Then the Hydrographic Survey, the Fisheries Protection Service, the Wireless Telegraph Service, the Tidal Survey, the Patrol of Northern Waters in Canada were under the Department of Marine and Fisheries. All these matters have oeen transferred to the Naval Service, and I think very properly transferred; but my hon. friend takes the consequences, he repudiates the principle. I do not know that he can justify himself or has answered successfully the criticisms of my friends behind me.

Is it the intention of the department to order the Canadian cadets, now on board the Berwick stationed at Bermuda, back to the Naval College at Halifax for a new course of one year? They are under examination at the present time. I am told that when their examinations are over they will be sent back for a new course at the Naval College at Halifax for one year. Is that the intention of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, the candidates who are now on the Berwick passing their examination will be sent back to the Naval College at Halifax for a one year's supplementary course.
Assuming that the Bill introduced by the hon. member for Mont-magny (Mr. Lesperance) passes, what will become of the Naval College?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have been taught that it is time enough to bid the devil good morning when you meet him. Perhaps the hon. gentleman might ask that question when the Bill passes.

This is a somewhat serious question. A certain number of young men of Canada have been induced, we might almost say, to enter upon a presumably naval career, and they did that in the first place believing that the Government intended to carry out a certain policy that had been laid down. These young men have sacrificed their time, they have sacrificed the prospects of their life in many cases, and I think it is reasonable to ask what is the prospect for them now? It is really a very serious matter to the young men themselves and to their families, if they are not to have the advantage of a career after they have trained for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I may say that an arrangement has been made under which those who have attained the rank of sub-lieutenant are serving now upon the British ships. The Naval College alt Halifax is being continued, the course there is being carried on, and as the young men graduate from there we hope that there will be an arrangement made by which we shall be able to place them in the Hydrographic Survey. One or two have been placed at their own request on the Hydrographic Survey, where practically we require men who have a knowledge of seamanship, which is very essential for hydrographic survey work. We propose to look after these young men and to see that no injustice is done to them.

Everybody will be glad to know that the Government is going to make arrangements that will be measurably satisfactory to these young men, but if the Government is going to maintain the Naval College at Halifax, it will mean the continuance of existing conditions. Is it intended to maintain that college with a view of furnishing a supply of Canadian officers-to the British navy?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That matter is being taken up at the present time, but it is hoped that-the Naval College will serve not only as a training college for men who want to follow the naval career, but also as a training.

school for men who want to follow other callings, such as the work in connection with the Hydrographic Survey and other work of that sort, just as the Military College at Kingston turns out men who follow other than military careers. Only a comparatively few of the graduates of the Military College embark on a military career, but the training that they get there fits them for other walks in life. Many become engineers and engage in other professions, and it is expected that the Naval College at Halifax will serve that purpose as well, so that the men will not only become naval officers and pursue a naval career but will be able to follow other lines of work with the education that they get there.

I do not think there will be a disposition to urge the Government too strongly upon this question. It will take a little time to wean them from the contribution policy in order that they may devote themselves to the development of Canada. They have been running in company with Mr. Churchill, and he is a pretty active man in getting around from one place to another. I see that the Canadian Naval Annual for this year says in so many words that the German scare was a thing that the people had to be weaned from, that it was all nonsense. It is the organ of the people who were making a great deal of the Herman scare just twelve months ago. Personally I feel that _we should be sympathetic to the Government in this matter. It will take a little time for them to wean themselves from the false line of policy they embarked in, but I hope they will become good Canadians and follow the example of New Zealand and Australia, without feeling they are very disloyal in being in such excellent company. I am perfectly sure they will come around to the idea of Canada being a good country within the empire, like the others. This hydrographic survey will no doubt work out very nicely; the country does not want the Government to go too fast with it, and if the hydrographic survey means an easy transition from the contribution policy, to the old policy they never should have abandoned, we should be patient with them. I would appeal to my hon. friend from Edmonton <Mr. Oliver) to take my point of view and allow the minister to get those Estimates, on this kind of provisional understanding.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am glad that what the
Government is doing in this direction has such a valiant defender in the person of my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark).

I am not an expert
in this matter, but I am quite interested in it because my son has the honour to be in the navy, studying the best way to defend his country and the empire if need be. Am I to understand that he will have to go back to the naval college? The expense to me has been quite heavy for the past two years, and I would like to know from the minister if I shall have to pay my son's expenses for another year.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: On the contrary, I do not think the son of my hon. friend will have any expense at all. If he becomes an officer he will receive a salary.
That is satisfactory.

To-night, my hon.
friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) referred to the fact that the Niobe had been tied up to a wharf at Halifax during the whole season, and for aught we know the Rainbow may have been similarly tied up to some wharf on the Pacific coast. I would like to know how many men are on the Niobe and Rainbow and what these ships are really supposed to be doing? It would seem, from what the minister has said tonight that the Government does not intend to go any iurther with the Canadian Naval Service, for he told us that the cadets were to find places in the British navy when their period of study was over. If the Government has abandoned the idea of a Canadian navy, it is difficult for me to understand why we should vote this money at all. What necessity is there for keeping up a staff of officers and voting $30,000 or $40,000 to pay their salaries, if these officers are to have nothing to do? The minister should give us some information as to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
More than two-thirds of this vote is for fishery protection, hydrographic survey, and other services which come under the Naval Department. We have to take care of the dockyards at Halifax and Esquimalt, under the arrangement- entered into with the British Government when these dockyards were handed over to Canada. There is a staff in each of these dockyards, and the vessels of the fishery protection fleet and other Government vessels are repaired there. Then we are continuing the Naval Service at Halifax, and that involves certain clerical aid at headquarters and elsewhere, and there is certain work to do in connection with the Niobe and Rainbow. There are about 150 men on the Niobe and a lesser number on the Rainbow, and they having -been

engaged for a ceiitain number of years we have to keep faith with them. In reply to the contention that there is no need for [DOT]a naval service department under certain conditions, I may say that if the Naval Service were abolished altogether there would be no saving as far as Civil Government Estimates are concerned, because there are not now enough employees in the Marine and Fisheries Department to take over the work in connection with the naval college, the dockyards, the hydrographic survey, fisheries protection and other similar services. The only thing that possibly might be saved would be the salary of a deputy minister, but I would ask hon. members to bear in mind that the Marine and Fisheries Department deals with a greater variety of subjects chan perhaps any other department of Government. While there are other departments of Government that are responsible for the expenditure of a larger sum of money during the year, still the Department of Marine, including the Naval Service, has a greater variety of subjects to deal -with than any other. It is very doubtful if, in view of the large increase in work in that department of late years, it would be possible to get along as one department, and my experience is that it would be necessary under any circumstances to have a division of the department with two deputy heads. Years ago when the work of the department was very much less than it is to-day, there was a deputy minister of marine and a deputy minister of fisheries. That system was abolished, but since then there have been added to the department a great many services that were unthought of years ago. Even if the Naval Service Department were abolished, it is doubtful if all the work of the department could be carried on with one deputy head.

While the explanation of the minister is very full and lucid, he will, I think, admit that from the viewpoint of the Opposition a naval service department without a navy is fairly and reasonably a subject of question. The hon. gentleman drew a parallel between the conditions of naval education and the conditions of military education, both of which are given by the Government. There is a vast difference. In the case of military education we have a permanent military force, and besides we have a very large volunteer force.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I think comparatively few
of our graduates at Kingston go into the permanent service.

Possibly. But at least we have the field for their abilities when they have secured the education they seek. But much the larger field, no doubt, is in connection with the volunteer force. There is a vast field of usefulness for the young men who have gone through the Kingston Military College in the line of life for which that education specially fits them. They know, before they enter the college, what the conditions are in regard to employment ir>
that line of life for which they are educating themselves. But in the case of the naval cadets they entered upon their course of instruction in the full belief that there was for them a Canadian Naval career; now, as my hon. friend has explained, we have everything in connection with the service except a navy, and the young men who have been prepared to sarcifice their time and talents in the interests of the Naval Service are left in a position that is unfortunate for them and not creditable to the Government. I think that we are fairly entitled to know what is the Government's intention in regard to the two vessels they have on their hands. Are they going to keep them in commission, or are they going to put them out of commission? Are these vessels to be tied up to the wharf, one in Halifax and the other in Esquimalt, with a partial complement of men, and neither fit for one thing nor fit for another? If that is the intention of the Government I think we are entitled to know it, and to know it now on this vote. We are voting $30,000 for the Civil Government expenses of the Canadian Navy. Now, if there is not going to be a navy, their ought not to be tliis vote. My hon. friend has explained, as he best of all men can explain, that we will need the money anyway, and that we have work to be done in other lines. That does not answer the question. We have this Naval Service, we have these two vessels; they are either fit for service or not fit for service. Is the Government keeping them fit for service, does it intend to keep them fit for service, does it intend to carry out the policy that was the reason for the establishment of the Naval College and for the purchase of these two vessels, namely, to carry out the policy of fitting young Canadians to take positions of responsibility in a navy owned, controlled and manned by Canada? I think that on this vote we are entitled to get a definite statement from

the minister as to the intentions of the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Niobe and the Rainbow have both been kept in a good state of repair, they have not been allowed to deteriorate; they are in quite as good a condition, if not better, than they were at [DOT] the time they were acquired by the Government of Canada. As to what disposition will be made of these vessels, that matter is under consideration at this time. It is doubtful whether the Rainbow could be disposed of at any price, if it were thought desirable to sell her, either to the British naval authorities or to any other such a body, for such a vessel would not be required in connection with a modern navy. It is doubtful also if anything could be obtained for the Niobe. It may be that the British Government would allow us to hand them back and take them off our hands, but whether we could sell them is a matter of some doubt, and it is receiving attention at the present time. The hon. gentleman asks me to state what the policy of the Government is to be in relation to naval affairs. He knows that the Prime Minister of Canada, who is the one, in circumstances of this sort, to enunciate the policy of the Government, has told this House on several occasions that before the country embarks upon a naval policy, that policy will be stated to the House and the people will be asked' whether they approve or disapprove. In view of that statement made by the Prime Minister on several occasions, I think the hon. gentleman will admit that it is not altogether right or proper to suggest that I should state to-night what the naval policy of the Government is to be, and no one more than the hon. gentleman would recognize the impropriety of my making such a statement. '

I do not see that there can be any question as to the propriety of the inquiry made by my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver). That hon. gentleman probably had in mind the answers given by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to a series of questions asked two years ago with respect to the appeal of the Naval Service Act. In those replies the minister statid that the Naval Service Act would be repealed. He further stated that after consulting the Admiralty this Government would announce its permanent naval policy and would appeal to the people upon it. Now, this Government did consult the Admiralty, but it did not announce its naval policy to the country, and it has taken no

steps, so far, to consult the people about it. So, in view of the replies given to the questions by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, I think it was quite natural for my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) to ask these questions to-night. And the minister, iE he were to look round him, would see that there is a great interest taken in this question by his friends and supporters from the province of Quebec. In fact the new member for Chateauguay (Mr. Morris) has moved several seats nearer to the minister to hear what is going on-no doubt with a view to enlightening the electors to whom he is alleged to have made some statements on this subject.

The minister has
stated that there are over one hundred men on the Niobe in Hali.ax. These men, I suppose, are undergoing some kind of naval training. But what kind of naval training do these men get aboard a ship tied to a wharf? Would not an essential part of their naval training be the efficient management of the ship and other matters which could only be learned at sea? These men are kept there at considerable expense to the country, and I doubt very much their obtaining any training that will be of any advantage to the country, or possibly to themselves. If it is the intention of the Government to repeal the Naval Service Act, could not some arrangement be made with these men whereby they could go into other walks of life and obtain a training that would be of s me use to thei ? It seems to me that the keeping of a large body of men under these circumstances, at very great expense to the country, is a useless waste. If these men must be kept there comparatively speaking in idleness, and it may be under cond.tions that may be disadvantageous, the whole thing appears to be a most peculiar arrangement.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The men who are now on these ships enlisted in Great Britain at the time the ships came out here. In war vessels of this nature there is a large amount of machinery of the most complicated character. Some of these men are ablebodied seamen, but a great many of them possess qualifications for taking care of that complicated machinery. These men were enlisted for a certain period of time which has not yet expired, and we are bound to retain them until that term expires. In any case it is necessary that they should be retained in the ship for the purpose of taking care of it, seeing that it does not deteriorate and that the

machinery is kept in proper order. A large number of the men on the ships are doing that work at the present time.

What did it cost last
year to maintain the Niobe and the Rainbow?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have not that information at hand, because I did not anticipate questions of that nature coming up on the Civil Government Estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's suggestion will have every consideration, I can assure him.

I must confess that there are a few things about the Niobe and the Rainbow that I do not quite understand. The minister tells us that it would be quite impossible at the present time either to give away these ships or to get anything
for them. That means that the ships are no good for anything, and if they are no good for anything, it is impossible for them to deteriorate. Why, therefore, should we spend our good money in keeping one hundred men on board the Niobe at Halifax if the ship is good for nothing, and if the Government find it impossible to obtain one cent for it ? Why should we pay one hundred men, out of the revenues of this country, to keep this worthless piece of machinery from deteriorating ? It does not sound to me like good business. I think that what the minister had in view in saying that we could not get rid of these ships was to show that the Laurier Administration had made a mistake, and had bought these ships when they were no good. They were certainly no good as instruments of war when they were taken over to this country. That was not the intention. The intention was that they should be used as training ships; that on these ships our young Canadians should learn something about the running of a cruiser, its machinery, and the processes of navigating it. I am in the very same position as the hon. member for Red Deer. If the ships are not worth a cent, why spend $20,000 to keep worthless articles from deteriorating ? It is bad business.

I think I may justify the question I asked- the minister by the remarks made by the hon. member for Cape Breton. I did not intend to ask for a declaration of the Government's naval policy; I did intend to ask what the intentions of the Government were in regard to the Niobe and the Rainbow. As the hon. member for Cape Breton has said, these vessels were bought to be used for the education of the young men who wished to enter upon a naval career; to give them an opportunity of being instructed in practical seamanship and the practical working of a man-of-war. The minister has informed us to-night that the young men who have enlisted are to be .given positions, some in the British navy, and some in the hydrographic survey, and the inference is that there is to be no naval career for Canadians. We are asked to vote money for clerical assistance to carry on the Naval Service, when we have no navy, and so far as we can judge, no intention on the part of the Government to have one. We have two vessels which are an enormous bill of expense to the country, serving no purpose, so far as I can see. If the Government were making a large expenditure of any other kind every year for

absolutely no purpose, certainly their action would be called into question. I am sure my hon. friend the minister must be prepared to make a statement in the matter.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder why the country should go on expending money on the navy, why the committee should pass this item.
I would have been pleased to hear from the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Nan-tel) and from the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Sevigny) two former members of the Nationalist party; I would like to know their opinion on the question.
On this side of the House, we speak freely on the naval policy, but our hon. friends opposite, are dumb. The hon. minister of Marine and Fisheries is the only one who dares answer our questions.
What are the sentiments of Mr. Lespe-rance, concerning this vote?
Would you be surprised, Mr. Speaker, to hear what the hon. member for Dorchester had to say during the last by-election, in Chateauguay, in October last? He was saying that the Niobe and the Rainbow were two old tubs, that they were good for nothing.
And now, the Government is asking the Committee to vote money for the maintenance of those old tubs. That is not fair.
The hon. member for Montmagny (Mr. Lesperanee) wants the repeal of the Naval service Act. I will support his Bill with both hands. What is the use of voting this money, just now? Let us, wait till after the Bill asking the repeal of the naval service Act is passed, and then the Niobe and the Rainbow can be sent back to England and be disposed of as scrap iron.
For my part, I strongly and formally oppose this expenditure. If the boats are nothing but old tubs, let them go to pieces.

(Translation). Mr. Speaker, ohe might have supposed that the hon. member for Montcalm (Mr. Lafortune) had said enough when he spoke for four hours or five hours on that question, last year, to dispense with the remarks he has just made.
I am surprised at the stand he now takes after having voted in 1910 for the Naval Service Act, at the bidding of the Laurier government-a law authorizing the construction of a navy which comprised twelve or fifteen boats.
If it happened to be the intention of the present government to .continue the policy 
introduced by the Administration of which my honorable friend was a supporter, he should exhibit to-day the same courage as in 1910, instead of going back on what he did and said at that time. The hon. member should at least wait till the Government dispose of these two boats which they have inherited from their predecessors.
Last summer I had the occasion to pay a visit to Halifax and to have a look at the now famous Niobe. The hon member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) wanted to know from the hon. minister of Marine and Fisheries why this boat has been kept in idleness, tied up to the.wharf, in the port of Halifax. The Niobe has been kept in idleness for the simple reason that there was nothing for her to do, and that is the best proof that Canada does not want a single battleship, and much less a dozen of them.
If the naval policy of the Liberal Government had gone through, we would have, by now, twelve or fifteen boats tied up at wharfs and the situation would be much worst than it is.
All that goes to show that Canada has no use for a navy and that if we are bound to do something, the policy of the present Government, the policy of a substantial contribution, is the wisest of the two.

Will the Government say if the hon. gentleman has cor-
9 P-m. rectly expressed the policy of the Government, that they will do nothing?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Will my hon. friend translate what was said?
The purport of it was that he approved of the policy of the Government in doing nothing.

Nothing has been said in answer to the remarks of hon. gentle-ment on this side as to the question of the repeal of the Naval Service Act. Two years ago a question was asked by the hon. member for Dorchester and after a long period of deliberation the Government replied that they would repeal the Naval Service Act. There is a Bill now before the House standing for its second reading to that effect and if the Government intends to adopt that Bill, introduced by one of its prominent supporters, it seems to me that we should not pass this item until we know whether fhey have made up their minds in regard to that matter. If this Bill should pass I
January 30,1914
think it will involve a reorganization of the whole question and will dispense with the employment of some of the officers for whom we are providing by this vote. The minister has not given any light on that question. I think we ought to have an answer as to whether the Government really intend to support the measure before the House or repeal the Naval Service Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think my hon.
friend or any other hon. member would seriously suggest that the Government should say what its policy is going to be on a certain Bill introduced by a private member before the Bill comes up for consideration. I cannot believe that my hon. friend is serious in asking that question. When the Bill comes down for consideration at the proper time, the policy of the Government will undoubtedly be stated by the First Minister or some other minister on behalf of the Government. For me to state now what the policy of the Government would be would be not only improper but not a course that any hon. member would approve.

I would not have ventured to ask this question had it not been that the policy of the Government was announced two years ago. I presume the Government are prepared to carry out the promise they then made to repeal the Naval Service Act. If the Government have changed their policy in that matter, of course I am out of order in asking the question. Is the policy of the Government the same to-day as when a reply was given in Parliament a couple of years ago that the Naval Service Act was to be repealed?
The Government has stated that the men who are engaged on the Niobe and Rainbow have been engaged in the old country for a term of years. How much longer are they to remain in the employ of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Deputy Minister tells me that these men were engaged for different periods, the longest period would be for five years beginning three years ago.
If I understand the situation it is that the Niobe and the Rainbow are tied up at wharfs.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They are in the harbours.

They are not cruising they are not being used for the purpose for which they were originally intended. The reason that they are kept in commission at all is to provide a place of employment for
some men, the balance of whose term of employment is two or three years and whose present occupation is looking after the delicate instruments which are used on these vessels. I would suggest to the minister that these men who are so employed are at the very best time in their lives, the time when they ought not only to be in the best kind of employment but when they should be doing the best service for themselves or for Canada or for Britain or for somebody and that they must be in a condition, if not of idleness at least of useless employment in keeping instruments in repair. The instruments must be kept in repair, but there is surely no reason why those instruments should be kept on the Niobe or Rainbow if the only purpose is to keep them in repair. If those ships are not to be used for their original purpose, they had better be dismantled and the men paid off.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend, I think, must to some extent have misunderstood me. I did not say that we were keeping instruments on board the boat, but the machinery which could not be removed. The men, the Deputy Minister informs me, are kept busy. The great bulk of them are Englishmen who have been in the English navy, and the Deputy Minister says they are kept employed. We are responsible for carrying out our contract with the men and if we dismiss them at an earlier date than the contract calls for some arrangement would have to be made to compensate the men.
Can the minister tell me what was the cost of the Niobe and the Rainbow?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have not the figures here and the Deputy Minister tells me he does not remember, but perhaps some of my hon. friends who were members of the Gov-ment at the time those ships were bought, have some recollection.

The point I wanted to
establish is this: a very large amount of the country's money is tied up in these vessels, their maintenance is costing a large amount of money, and the purpose for which the money was voted is not being carried out. And so far as we can learn from the minister, it is not the intention of the Government to carry it out. The country, meanwhile, is burdened with that expense, capital and current, without any reason whatever. We have asked, we have almost badgered, the minister for an answer as to

what the Government intends to do in the matter. I think we have keen strictly within pur rights in asking these questions, and I am very much disappointed that the Government is not able or willing to give us a *dear and straightforward answer. The matter is one that I think is seriously contentious, and I think that what has passed across the floor to-night is sufficient evidence on that point. I think my hon. friend will remember that when the leader of the Government and the leader of the Opposition spoke last night as to the business that was to be taken up to-day, it was understood that any of the Estimates that were contentious would not be proceeded with. This certainly has developed into a contentious matter and in view of the understanding between the leaders I would respectfully ask my hon. friend to allow it to stand over.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I hope my hon. friend did not gather from any remark of mine that I wished to imply that the Opposition were asking questions that were improper from the standpoint of an opposition. I fully realize what the rights and duties of an opposition are, and make no complaint whatever about any inquiries made of me when my Estimates are before the House. I have endeavoured to give such answers as I thought would be satisfactory to my hon. friends opposite. Having been in opposition myself in a legislature for nine years, 1 know it is sometimes difficult to satisfy an opposition with information, and very frequently if the Government gives information it is not considered satisfactory by those opposed to the Government. My hon. friend surely does not expect me to state what the naval policy is. That is a matter for the Prime Minister when the proper time comes. I have given my hon. friend all the information I can with regard to these vessels and the number of men employed on them, and with regard to the work these men are doing, I have also told my hon. friend that so far as the question of disposing of these vessels is concerned, no conclusion has been reached. The matter is being carefully considered by the department and will be considered by the Government when the department is in a position, after consideration with its officials, to make a report to the Government on that matter. I do not know what further information I can give my hon. friend. I would have no hesitation in allowing the item to stand, but I think my hon. friend should have asked that it stand over when the question first came up. I would have

agreed to that without a moment's hesitation. But here we have been discussing for an hour, almost, every phase of the question and.I have answered all questions as far as I am able except the one asking the cost of the Niobe and Rainbow. Under these circumstances I ask my hon. friend if he thinks the item ought to stand? If my hon. friend and his friends want the item to stand and say so, I am not going to insist upon its being passed to-night. I would point out, however, that when the main Naval Estimates come before the House at a later day, there will be the fullest possible opportunity for discussion of this question, and I will be delighted to give hon. gentlemen all the information possible if they desire to go on with the matter at that time.
'Mr. OLIVER: I am sure my hon. friend is courteous and considerate in every respect, and I do not wish him to think I have any fault to find with his attitude on this matter. But my hon. friend the member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) before he went away this evening, asked that the item should stand and in view of the fact that it has developed into a contentious item and in view of the arrangements which I understand existed bet\een the two leaders last night, I would ask that the item stand for the present, and in making that request I do not want the minister to understand that I am making any criticism whatever of him or of the way in which he has dealt with this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I think I understand the attitude of the hon. member for Edmontm, and if it is his desire that the item should stand, I will at once agree; but if we are to go over all this again on some future occasion, I think it is unfortunate that the matter did not develop as contentious before dinner. However, if that is the hon. gentleman's request I will bow to it.
Civil Government-Department of Militia and Defence-Salaries and contingencies, $186,900.

Will the hon. minister explain?
Hon. SAM. HUGHES (Minister of Militia and Defence): There- are no increases except the statutory increases.
What is included in that item of sundries, $ 11,000 ? Is that another trip to England?

No trip to England.
When the main Estimates come up, I shall

be delighted to give my hon. friend the particulars about that trip to England, and I am sure he will regret that he was not along and that he had not become a soldier earlier in life.
What are the sundries for?
They are for general odds and ends and for travelling expenses.
What are some of the items?
The travelling expenses of civil officers of the Department come out of that.
I do not want to be persistent at all, but it seems to me the Minister's explanations are rather vague-odds and ends.
These are travelling expenses.
Is that $11,000 made up of small items?
All small items-the expenses of officers travelling to Toronto, Quebec or anywhere. These are civil officers, not the military department.

It was explained by the hon. Minister's colleague, the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), in connection with an item for sundries under the head of contingencies, that the item of travelling expenses which used to be voted in connection with a special appropriation had been transferred to this item of sundries under the head of contingencies, and that his Estimates were thereby increased by that amount. The estimates of the hon. Minister of Militia, under the head of sundries, apparently remain the same as they were last year. The Minister of Militia is not following in his department the custom as explained by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
I presume my hon. friend the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries is following our custom.
No.
We have always had our expenses for travel under this head. I do not know what the Naval Service is doing at all. I am not running that show; I am running this show.

I would like to ask the minister if this item of sundries would cover, for instance, the travelling and other incidental expenses of entertaining the 22
visiting officers, say, from England, whom the Minister of Militia might see fit to entertain as properly he should. Would it also cover the expense of a visiting officer if the minister takes him to a political picnic, for instance, wearing a badge ' Britain and the Empire,' where a visiting British officer would hardly be expected to feel particularly at home in a country where all classes of the people are supposed to be loyal to the empire to which we are all so proud to belong. I would like to know if that is the case.

If the Minister of Militia
entertains an officer, he entertains him himself. He does not charge him up to the public expense. If the Minister of Militia takes a gentleman to any party-Queenston Heights I presume my hon. friend refers to-he does so at his own expense and assumes the full responsibility for it. If he wears a badge, the Minister of Militia and Defence is responsible for the wearing of his badge. He asks no person what badge he shall wear on such an occasion.

I am not worried about
what badge the minister wears; we all know the badge he wears. That is not a matter of any particular concern. I am asking whether this $11,000 for sundries would cover such an occasion as where the minister takes a foreign officer, or an officer from the old country, or any other country, to a picnic. Does the minister mean to tell us that the minister pays the expenses of the visitors, because I have no fault to find with that proposition; but, in connection with the particular incident that he referred to, did the minister actually pay out of his own pocket the expenses of this visiting officer, and does he pay the expenses of visiting officers while travelling through the country?

The hon. gentleman referred to an incident that occurred at a picnic at Queenston Heights. I take the responsibility of everything that occurred on that occasion. When General Ian Hamilton travelled through this country as Inspector General, all his expenses were paid out of the general vote, but that has nothing to do with Civil Government, nor had the incident to which my hon. friend refers anything to do with this item.

If this incident does not
come under this item, that is all I want from the minister. But the minister will understand, of course, that when we do



come to the point we hope the matter may be properly discussed.
I shall be glad to give my hon. friend the opportunity.
We would like to have a little information about that particular trip to Queenston Heights.
The Minister's explanation is that this $11,000 would simply cover the travelling expenses of officers of the department9
The civil officers.
The civil officers; that is the only explanation of the expenditure of this $11,000?
That is the great bulk of it.
Would $9,000 be a fair estimate of the travelling expenses?
I think it would be more than that.

I am sorry that my military experience is not very large, but it would appear to me as a rank outsider that the amount of $11,000 for the travelling expenses of the civil staff of the department is too large. I do not appreciate how the civil end of the military department has to do so much travelling. I understand that the travelling was generally done by the military officers, not by the civil officers.

If that question had been asked by some hon. gentleman on the other side who had never sat within the sacred precincts of the Privy Council, we would not have wondered at it; but the item is the same item that the hon. gentleman passed himself whilst he was a minister sitting with his colleagues around the Council Board. I do not think that it has been increased at all from the time that he passed it himself. It is the same item that has been passed for years.

The minister compliments the Government too much.
. Mr. SINCLAIR: In looking at the Auditor General's Report I find that the contingencies under the Civil Government item for the Department of Militia and Defence last year amounted to $22,028. I do not know whether this represents the same expenditure or not, but the amount is more than twice as much as the item we are discussing.
fMr. Neely. 1
If the hon. gentleman looks at the Estimates he will see that the vote includes contingencies, clerical assistance, printing and stationery and sundries.
Is it the same expenditure that we are discussing now?

We are discussing one of the three items which go to make up the whole of the contingencies. If the hon. gentleman will turn to page 13 of his Estimates he will see that the vote includes these three items.

.Does the Minister of Militia intend shortly to make provision for the payment of the Fenian bounty claims? I, and others, have had numerous inquiries with regard to this matter. A great many have put in their claims, and the statement having gone abroad that the Act expired on the 31st December, the claimants are uneasy as to whether or not their claims will be paid.

It is the intention of the Government to taken any legislation that may be necessary to continue the right of any claimant who may have presented his claim. There are a number of questions on the Order Paper with reference to this matter, and they will be answered in due course. I may say now that every claim that has been allowed will be paid. The Militia Department has nothing to do with paying the claims; it merely issues a warrant and the Finance Department pays.
Civil Government-Department of the Interior-Salaries and contingencies, $1,258,255.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. J. ROCHE (Minister of the Interior) :
speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The statutory increases amount to $33,357, and the other increases, caused by increased clerkships, to $83,700, being a total of $116,957. There have been decreases through the filling of vacancies occasioned by promotion, resignations, &c. In all cases, the new clerks came in at the minimum of the salary of the division to which they were promoted.

There seems to be a
large increase in the contingencies for travelling expenses?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: That is occasioned by the fact that the travelling expenses, which formerly -were paid out of the votes for the different services, will in future be paid out ot this vote.
Does the total represent any actual increase over last year ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: These Estimates are based on the Estimates of last year.
Apparently, there is an increase of about 88 officials.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The hon. gentleman, who was formerly minister of this department, will appreciate the explanation of that. The department has over 800 employees, and during the course of the year there have been employed from 70 to 145 temporary clerks at different periods. Under the present practice, temporary employees are only allowed to remain in the department for six months. Formerly, when they were in a department for six months and did not pass the examination they were transferred to another department in which they remained for the next six months, and so on. That practice has been abolished, and now, unless they have passed their examination within the first six months they are compelled to leave the service, and usually just at the time when they are becoming proficient in their work. I consulted the heads of the different branches, and in order to avoid the employment of so many temporary employees, it was considered it would be very much better in the interests of the service and in the interests of economy, that we should have a larger number of permanent employees. Of course we must continue to take some vote for temporary clerical assistance, but it will be materially reduced.
This is really only an apparent increase ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: That is all.
I took objection a short time ago to the passing of the Estimates for the Naval Department, but in order to facilitate business it may be well to withdraw the objection and let the item go through.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Thank you.
On the understanding that discussion may be had when the other naval Estimates come up.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes.
Civil Government-Department of Labour- Salaries, $52,412.50 ; contingencies, $15,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. W. CROTHERS (Minister of Labour):
speechtext:
Hon. members will notice that there is an inc ease of one in the staff of the department, and of $700 in the amount devoted to salaries. The new appointee is a messenger. This appointment and the statutory increases explain the increase of $700. The contingencies are the same as last year.

I have received c.mmu-nications to the effect that a statement appears in our papers that a new Bill is being introduced to extend the Industrial Disputes Act so as to co er all classes of employment. I have a question on the Order Paper for Monday on that subject, but I .should be glad if the minister could give me the information now.
There will be an itjui later on for the administration of the Industrial Disputes Act, and perhaps my hon. friend will wait until that time. It would be more in order to discuss such a matter then.

Will that be reached
this evening?

I suppose not; we are only taking up Civil Government now.
Civil Government-Department of Inland Revenue-Salaries, $182,087-50 ; contingencies, $10,000.
Will the Minister of Inland Revenue be good enough to explain the increase of size in the membership of the staff?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. B. NANTEL (Minister of Inland Revenue):
speechtext: We have an Assistant Deputy Minister, Mr. J. U. Vincent at a sa'ary of $3,350. Then, in the branch of Dr. McGill, Chief Analyst, we have two analysts employed, Mr. Dawson and Mr. Papineau Couture.
What is the increase in the Weights and Measures branch?
We have a chief inspector, Mr. Way, who last year was assistant chief and has now been promoted. His salary is $2,800.

Who is the present
deputy minister?
Mr. W. Himsworth.
Is he retiring?
He will retire soon, but is still in office.
When does he retire?
Probably next spring.
About what date?
About April, I suppose.
Who is to succeed him?
That is not decided yet, but there is the assistant deputy minister, Mr. Vincent, who has been appointed cum futura successione.

Under 'Sundries' there
is an increase of $1,000. What is that for?
'Sundries' covers unforseen expenditure, such as subscriptions to newspapers, telephones, telegrams, etc.
Subscriptions to newspapers?

Yes, there are many in
my department.
I know that people subscribe to newspapers that they do not want, but I did not know that the departments did.

They always have. It
was so when I took office.

Would the minister mind
telling us if he intends to introduce legislation to govern the manufacture, sale and use of explosives?
That is not in my department.

It was in the minister's
department last session.

It belongs to the Mines
Department.
May I ask if the revenue cutters that were referred to this afternoon are in this department?
No, they are in the Customs Department.

I wanted to find that
out because I have had some difficulty in locating them.

I have nothing to do
with them.

How many inspectors
of weights and measures are there in the province of Nova Scotia, and what are their names and salaries?

That is in the outside
service, and I have not the notes on that subject with me. But I am informed that there are three inspectors in Nova Scotia.

I think the question
will be in order now:	Some of the retail
merchants are complaining of inspection of their weights and measures being made oftener than is necessary, and the inspectors compel them to pay a fee for this inspection. There is a certain amount of trouble and friction about it, and I desired to ask the minister whether he proposes to change the law so as to relieve the retail men of the charge now made

upon them for inspection of weights and measures.

I have received no complaint as to that.
'Mr. J. J. HUGHES: These inspectors of weights and measures are paid by the Government, and they also exact a pretty large fee.
The fee is not large; it has not been changed since I took office.
Where do the fees go?
The fees go to the department.

I desire to take thi# opportunity of thanking the minister for giving heed to a request which I made of him last year. I made many requests of the Government for various small things, but the Minister of Inland Revenue was the only member of the Government who heeded my requests. Last year I brought to his attention the matter of an employee of his department at Halifax, Mr. Patrick Tompkins, who had been in the employ of the department for twenty years, and was getting a very small salary. I wish to thank the Minister of Inland Revenue very kindly for having granted this gentleman the increase of pay which he so well deserved.

I understand that the
Deputy Minister of the Department is leaving some time in the spring, and that another gentleman, Mr. Vincent, is taking his place. How long has this gentleman been in the service of the department, and what qualifications has he for the office?

Mr. Vincent has been in the department since last October. He has been recognized by Mr. fehortt, of the Civil Service Commission, as being capable of filling the position; I consider he is well qualified for the office. Probably he will be appointed deputy minister.
What was his occupation before he entered the service of the department?

He was a lawyer in
Ottawa. A lawyer should make a good deputy minister for the Department of Inland Revenue.
Civil Government-Department of Agriculture-Salaries and contingencies, $509,637.50.
Will the hon. minister explain the increase in the staff and the increase in the salaries?

There will be two vacancies created by promotion of two officers into the first division. The four patent examiners in that division, who have practically reached the maximum of $2,100 in the second division, are going up from the $2,100 to $2,800 class. Two men have been brought in from the outside service and appointed field husbandman and seed analyst respectively. In the next division the four vacancies are created by promotions, and four of the patent office who have been in the $1,200 to $1,600 class will be promoted to the $1,600 and $2,100 class. Most of these patent examiners come in on probation at $1,200, on the stipulation that they shall go up to $1,600 after the first year, if their services are satisfactory. In addition to that we are providing for an assistant. Dominion botanist., a horticulturist, another clerk in the copyrights branch, an assistant editor in the publications branch, and an assistant Dominion entomologist. In .subdivision B we have a number of vacancies and are providing for the appointment of an assistant to the Dominion botanist, to the Dominion field husbandman, the transfer to the inside service of an outside officer, an additional clerk in the minister's office, an assistant to the Dominion chemist, a filing clerk in the publications office. In the third division some clerks who have reached their maximum in the $500 to $800 class are going up to the $900 to $1,200 class. The changes are simply the result of the natural expansion of departmental work, with the addition of the officers I have jjst mentioned.
Are the two positions at $5,000 new?

No. These are Dr.
Montizambert and Dr. Torrance.
Why are the travelling expenses so large this year?

Hitherto we have paid all our expenses from the votes apportioned to the different branches. It has been suggested that we should do away with that practice, and put these expenses into a general travelling expense fund for all branches. Many of the officers of the inside service of the department are travelling a good deal of the time, particularly those in
the experimental farm, dairy and cold stor age and live stock branches. This change was suggested by the Auditor General. Last year the amount was, I think, between $45,0f)0 and $50,000.
Have all the positions in subdivision ' A ' of the first division been filled?
No. This will provide for two promotions and a possible new appointment.
Are the vacancies in this subdivision to be filled by promotion?
Yes, some of them. I have spoken of the four in the patent examiners* branch. Four patent senior examiners who have reached their maximum of $2,100 will go into the $2,100 to $2,800 class.

What is the explanation
of the doubling of the vote for clerical and other assistance?

Last year we had a great deal of trouble because we 10 p. m. could not get permanent clerks from the Civil Service Commission to fill a lot of appointments, and we had to put on a number of temporary employees. We ran much behind our vote last year for temporary employees. If we had had permanent appointments for this, much of the vote would have lapsed. We had to increase our temporary vote, and we are providing enough so that if we do not get the permanent clerks we shall have enough to pay for temporary assistance.
Civil Government-Post Office Deaprtment- Salaries and contingencies, $867,810.

The number of officers is the
same, and the increase is due to statutory increases.
' Mr. MURPHY: What is the increase in contingencies?

To a large extent it
is due to the same reason given by other departments.
I notice an item for provisional allowances in the Northwest. What is the explanation of that?

That is a special allowance that we give in Western Canada, which existed before my time. The explanation is, and I do not hesitate to say this, that the law does not permit us to pay sufficient
.342

salaries to get good men in the West We get men and they leave the service because we are. not allowed by law to pay them sufficient salary. The late Government provided for this to a certain extent by making what they called a living allowance tc the employees in the West, that is from Winnipeg to the Coast. In a general way the allowance is $180, but it varies according to salary.
What class of employees get the benefit of that allowance5

For officers receiving $1,600 and under, $15 a month, that is $180 a year. In the case of salaries over $1,600 and under $1,780, the allowance is the amount required to make up a total of $1,780, this being the amount that would be received by a clerk whose salary is $1,600.
The dead letter effice employees of the West are part of the Inside Service?

Yes.
Civil Government-Public Works-Salaries and contingencies, $62S,547.50.

speakeroldname: Hon. ROBERT ROGERS (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext: I might say, in a general way, that there are no increases except the ordinary statutory increases, as far as I know, and a few7 promotions. The total amount asked this year is $543,000 as against $527,000, or a difference of $16,000 for the general increase incident to the expansion of the department made up entirely of the natural increase and statutory increases.

In the second division,
subdivision 'A,' I see two more have been appointed, and in the second division, subdivision ' B ' five more.

These are the increases
incident to the development and extra work of the department.
What is the meaning of that item in the second division subdivision ' A ' where it says ' remainder of salary in Estimates of Railways and Canals'?
That refers to D. A. McLaughlin, the photographer. He gets part of his salary from my department, and the rest from the Railway Department.
Travelling expenses have increased by $46,000.

The same answer applies to that as was given by my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture. Heretofore, if we

sent out an inspector, an engineer or purchasing agent his expenses were chargeable to the particular work on which he was engaged, but for some reason or other on the recommendation of the Auditor General or Treasury Board, that has been changed and all travelling expenses are charged to a contingency account. That accounts for the increase over last year.
How would the various items compare with this year?
About the same I think.

There is a considerable
increase in the printing and stationery. Is there any explanation of that?

Printing and stationery
last year was $12,500 and this year $17,000, The increase is due to books, publications and so on.

Has it anything to do
with newspaper advertising?
I do not think so.

Where is the printing
being done?
In the Printing Bureau.
Have many new clerks been appointed by the department during the last year?

Very few; about four or five additional ones in the different offices.

speechtext: No. One officer has been dropped. Moreover, the officer tvho last year combined the duties of secretary and assistant deputy minister was paid $5,000. This year we are paying the gentleman who replaces him only $4,000. We have diminished, not increased, the number of officers.
